title: Future housing demand turns climate resilience into a household-wealth, fiscal-capacity, and spatial-inequality problem
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11451, Housing Requirements, Hazard Exposure, and Resilience Costs: A Global Outlook to 2100
geography: Global country-level and subnational housing-demand, demographic, construction, hazard-exposure, and fiscal-capacity projections to 2100

observations.period: 2025-2100; projected global housing stock and construction demand

denominator.unit: global housing-stock projection under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway scenarios

growth_to_replacement.value: construction demand in most regions transitions from growth-driven to replacement-driven by mid-century

household_wealth_route.value: housing is both a major component of household wealth and a major component of national capital stock

mechanism.value: where and how housing is built now shapes future hazard exposure, repair and replacement costs, and fiscal obligations

observations.method: Integrated projection using Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, dynamic household-size modeling, cohort survival analysis, and housing-stock and construction-demand estimation.
observations.uncertainty: These are scenario-based long-horizon projections sensitive to population, household-size, urbanization, income, construction, hazard, and climate assumptions; they are not a forecast of realized units or costs.
observations.subgroup: Countries and regions with different demographic growth, urbanization, household-size change, construction systems, housing quality, and existing stock exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Replacement demand may be financed or delivered differently from new growth demand, and better housing quality or migration could change the projected stock and spatial distribution.

long_term_cost.value: resilient construction pathways carry lower long-term costs than business-as-usual in most regions

exception_regions.value: high-growth, high-hazard regions such as South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa do not uniformly show lower long-term resilient-construction costs under the modeled conditions

timing_problem.value: resilience requires higher or earlier construction decisions while benefits arrive through avoided future exposure and replacement costs

household_translation.value: upfront resilient standards can become housing prices, rents, public finance needs, or avoided future displacement and repair burden

observations.method: Modeled comparison of business-as-usual and resilient construction pathways using hazard exposure, housing quality, replacement-cost, and demographic scenarios.
observations.uncertainty: The relative cost result depends on hazard intensity, construction standards, discounting, financing, enforcement, housing-market response, and whether avoided losses are fully captured.
observations.subgroup: Low-income and high-growth households, renters and owners, governments, builders, lenders, insurers, and regions with different hazard and fiscal conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower modeled long-term cost does not guarantee that households or governments can finance the upfront investment; resilience standards can also raise near-term exclusion or affordability pressures if not accompanied by support.

observations.period: 2025-2100; countries facing combined housing, hazard, and fiscal constraints

denominator.unit: countries identified with high future housing demand, severe natural-hazard exposure, and limited fiscal capacity

triple_burden.value: 46 countries face the combined burden of high future housing demand, severe natural-hazard exposure, and limited fiscal capacity to finance resilient construction

regional_pattern.value: Pacific Island countries face acute fiscal constraints, Sub-Saharan Africa faces unprecedented volumetric demand, and South and Southeast Asia face the highest hazard exposure

governance_route.value: housing adaptation becomes a coordination problem spanning land, construction, finance, infrastructure, disaster risk, social protection, and international support

distributional_risk.value: countries with the least fiscal room may face the largest future demand and exposure, turning climate resilience into a global inequality and dependency question

observations.method: Country and regional classification combining projected housing demand, multi-hazard exposure, and fiscal-capacity indicators.
observations.uncertainty: The triple-burden classification depends on thresholds, scenario choices, hazard data, fiscal measures, and the study's spatial aggregation; it identifies priority conditions rather than fixed rankings.
observations.subgroup: Pacific Island states, Sub-Saharan African countries, South and Southeast Asian countries, urban and rural populations, and households in fragile or under-resourced housing stock.
observations.counterinterpretation: International finance, migration, technology, building-material innovation, and domestic policy could alter the burden; fiscal capacity is not the same as political willingness or implementation capacity.

related_sources.claim: Bibliographic record and abstract for WPS11451, including global stock, pathway, regional, and 46-country triple-burden findings.
World Bank reproducibility package with verified computational reproduction and metadata.
Related-materials inventory describing hazard, housing, cost, subnational, and triple-burden outputs.
World Bank disaster-risk-management publication page listing the study.

boundary: This record adds long-horizon housing-resilience cost and triple-burden mechanisms linking climate exposure, demographic demand, fiscal capacity, household wealth, and infrastructure. It is scenario-based projection evidence, not a realized housing shortage, actual household affordability estimate, causal adaptation evaluation, or fixed country ranking.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank PDF, abstract record, reproducibility package, related-materials inventory, and disaster-risk publication page were reviewed for housing-stock projections, growth-to-replacement transition, resilient-versus-business-as-usual costs, regional exceptions, 46-country triple burden, and scenario boundaries.
